<poem> Winter is past; the heart of Nature warms Beneath the wrecks of unresisted storms; Doubtful at first, suspected more than seen, The southern slopes are fringed with tender green; On sheltered banks, beneath the dripping eaves, Spring’s earliest nurslings spread their glowing leaves, Bright with the hues from wider pictures won, White, azure, golden,—drift, or sky, or sun,— </poem><section end="s2" /><noinclude></noinclude>

{{rh|80|SONGS IN MANY KEYS|}} {{center block/s}}
Line after line, along the bursting sod,
Marks the broad acres where his feet have trod;
Still, where he treads, the stubborn clods divide,
The smooth, fresh furrow opens deep and wide;
Matted and dense the tangled turf upheaves,
Mellow and dark the ridgy cornfield cleaves;
Up the steep hillside, where the laboring train
Slants the long track that scores the level plain;
Through the moist valley, clogged with oozing clay,
The patient convoy breaks its destined way;
At every turn the loosening chains resound,
The swinging ploughshare circles glistening round,
Till the wide field one billowy waste appears,
And wearied hands unbind the panting steers. These are the hands whose sturdy labor brings
The peasant's food, the golden pomp of kings;
This is the page, whose letters shall be seen
Changed by the sun to words of living green;
This is the scholar, whose immortal pen
Spells the first lesson hunger taught to men;
These are the lines which heaven-commanded Toil
Shows on his deed,—the charter of the soil! O gracious Mother, whose benignant breast
Wakes us to life, and lulls us all to rest,
How thy sweet features, kind to every clime,
Mock with their smile the wrinkled front of time!
We stain thy flowers,—they blossom o'er the dead;
We rend thy bosom, and it gives us bread;
O'er the red field that trampling strife has torn,
Waves the green plumage of thy tasselled corn;
Our maddening conflicts sear thy fairest plain,
Still thy soft answer is the growing grain.
Yet, O our Mother, while uncounted charms
Steal round our hearts in thine embracing arms,
Let not our virtues in thy love decay,
And thy fond sweetness waste our strength away. No! by these hills, whose banners now displayed
In blazing cohorts Autumn has arrayed;
By yon twin summits, on whose splintery crests
The tossing hemlocks held the eagles' nests;
By these fair plains the mountain circle screens,
And feeds with streamlets from its dark ravines,—
True to then home, these faithful arms shall toil
To crown with peace their own untainted soil;
And, true to God, to freedom, to mankind,
If her chained bandogs Faction shall unbind,
These stately forms, that bending even now
Bowed their strong manhood to the humble plough,
Shall rise erect, the guardians of the land,
The same stern ion in the same right hand,
Till o'er their hills the shouts of triumph run,
The sword has rescued what the plough-share won! {{center block/e}}
{{c|{{larger|SPRING}}}} {{center block/s}} {{sc|Winter}} is past; the heart of Nature warms
Beneath the wrecks of unresisted storms;
Doubtful at first, suspected more than seen,
The southern slopes are fringed with tender green;
On sheltered banks, beneath the dripping eaves,
Spring's earliest nurslings spread their glowing leaves,
Bright with the hues from wider pictures won,
White, azure, golden,—drift, or sky, or sun,—

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> Heaven keep us all! Is every rascal
clown
Whose arm is strouger free to knock us down ?
Has every scarecrow, whose eachectic soul
Seems — from Bedlam, airing on pa- role,
Who, though he carries buf a doubtful trace
Of angel visits on his hungry face, *
From lack of marrow or the coins to pay,

The right to stick us with his cutthroat terms,
And bait his homilies with his brother worms? {{center block/e}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> The very bank of language broke, —
Such deeds, that Langhter nearly died
With stitches in his belted side;
While Time, caught fast in pleasure’s ehain,
His double goblet suupped in twain,
And stood with lalf in either hand, —
Both brimaning full, — but not of sand f
It may not be; J strive in vain
To break my slender household chain, — Three pairs of litile clasping hands,
One yoice, that whispers, not commands. Even while iy spirit flies away,
My gentle jailers murmur nay;
All shapes of elemental wrath
They raise along my threatened path; The storm grows black, the waters rise, The mountains mingle with the skies, The mad tornado acoops the ground, The midnight robber prowls around, — Thus, kissing every limb they tic,
They draw a knot and heave a sigh,
Tili, fairly netted in the toil,
My feet are rooted to the soil.
Only the soaring wish is free !—
And that, dear Governor, flies to thee } </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />TO AN ENGLISH FRIEND
<poem> The seed that wasteful autumn cast To waver on its stormy blast, Long o'er the wintry desert tost, Its living germ has never lost. Dropped by the weary tempest's wing, It feels the kindling ray of spring, And, starting from its dream of death, Pours on the air its perfumed breath.
So, parted by the rolling flood, The love that springs from common blood Needs but a single sunlit hour Of mingling smiles to bud and flower; Unharmed its slumbering life has flown, From short to shore, from zone to zone, Where summer's falling roses stain The tepid waves of Pontchartrain, Or where the lichen creeps below Katahdin's wreaths of whirling snow.
Though fiery sun and stiffening cold May change the fair ancestral mould, No winter chills, no summer drains The life-blood drawn from English veins, Still bearing whereso'er it flows The love that with its fountain rose, Unchanged by space, unwronged by time, From age to age, from clime to clime! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />AFTER A LECTURE ON WORDS- WORTH
[In 1853 Dr. Holmes gave a course of lea= tures before the Lowell Institute in Hoston on English Poetry of the Nineteenth Century, and this and the following five poems were pnat- ludes te the lectures. j
<poem> Come, spread your wings, as [ spread mine,
and leave the crowded hall For where the eyes of twilight shine
O'er evening’s western wall.
These are the pleasant Berkshire hills, Each with ita leafy erown;
Hark! from their sides a thousand rilla Come singing sweetly duwn,
A thousand rills; they leap und shine, Strained through the shadawy nooka,
Till, clasped in many a gathering twine, They swell a hundred brooks.
A hundred brooks, and still they run With ripple, shade, and gleam,
Til, clustering all their braids in one, They flow a single stream.
A bracelet apun from mountain mist, A silvery sash unwound,
With ox-bow curye and sinuous twist lt writhes te reach the Sound.
This is my bark,— a pygmy’s ship: Beneath a child it rolls:
Fenr uot, —one bady makea it dip, But net a thousand souls,
Float we the grassy banks between; Without an oar we glide;
The meadows, drest in living green, Unroll on either side.
Come, take the book we love so well, And let us read and dream
We see whate’er its pages tell, And sail an English stream.
Up to the clouds the lark has sprung, Still trilling us he flies; </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude></noinclude>

{{rh|90|SONGS IN MANY KEYS}} {{rule}} {{center block/s}}
The very bank of language broke,
Such deeds, that Laughter nearly died
With stitches in his belted side;
While Time, caught fast in pleasure's chain,
His double goblet suupped in twain,
And stood with half in either hand, -
Both brimming full, but not of sand! It may not be; I strive in vain-
To break my slender household chain,-
Three pairs of little clasping hands,
One voice, that whispers, not commands.
Even while my spirit flies away,
My gentle jailers murmur nay;
All shapes of elemental wrath
They raise along my threatened path;
The storm grows black, the waters riso,
The mountains mingle with the skies,
The mad tornado scoops the ground,
The midnight robber prowls around, -
Thus, kissing every limb they tie,
They draw a knot and heave a sigh,
Till, fairly netted in the toil,
My feet are rooted to the soil.
Only the soaring wish is free!--
And that, dear Governor, flies to thee! {{center block/e}}
{{c|TO AN ENGLISH FRIEND}} {{center block/s}} THE seed that wasteful autumn cast
To waver on its stormy blast,
Long o'er the wintry desert tost,
Its living germ has never lost.
Dropped by the weary tempest's wing,
It feels the kindling ray of spring,
And, starting from its dream of death,
Pours on the air its perfumed breath. So, parted by the rolling flood,
The love that springs from common blood
Needs but a single sunlit honr
Of mingling smiles to bud and flower;
Unharmed its slumbering life has flown,
From shore to shore, from zone to zone,
Where summer's falling roses stain
The tepid waves of Pontchartrain,
Or where the lichen ereeps below
Katahdin's wreaths of whirling snow. Though fiery sun and stiffening cold
May change the fair ancestral mould,
No winter chills, no summer drains
The life-blood drawn from English veins,
Still bearing whereso'er it flows
The love that with its fountain rose,
Unchanged by space, unwronged by time,
From age to age, from clime to clime! {{center block/e}}
{{c|AFTER A LECTURE ON WORDSWORTH}} {{fine block|[In 1853 Dr. Holmes gave a course of lectures before the Lowell Institute in Boston on English Poetry of the Nineteenth Century, and this and the following five poems were poatludes to the lectures.]}} {{center block/s}} COME, spread your wings, as I spread mine,
And leave the crowded hall
For where the eyes of twilight shine
O'er evening's western wall. These are the pleasant Berkshire hills,
Each with its leafy crown;
Hark from their sides a thousand rilla
Come singing sweetly down. A thousand rills; they leap and shine,
Strained through the shadowy nooks,
Till, clasped in many a gathering twine,
They swell a hundred brooks. A hundred brooks, and still they run
With ripple, shade, and gleam,
Till, clustering all their braids in one,
They flow a single stream. A bracelet spun from mountain mist,
A silvery sash unwound,
With ox-bow curve and sinuous twist
It writhes to reach the Sound.- This is my bark, a pygmy's ship:
Beneath a child it rolls;
Fear not, one body makes it dip,
But not a thousand souls. Float we the grassy banks between;
Without an oar we glide;
The meadows, drest in living green,
Unroll on either side. Come, take the book we love so well,
And let us read and dream
We see whate'er its pages tell,
And sail an English stream. Up to the clouds the lark has sprung,
Still trilling as he flies;
{{center block/e}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{rh|90|SONGS IN MANY KEYS}} {{rule}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{ppoem|start=follow| The very bank of language broke, Such deeds, that Laughter nearly died With stitches in his belted side; While Time, caught fast in pleasure's chain, His double goblet suupped in twain, And stood with half in either hand, - Both brimming full, but not of sand!
It may not be; I strive in vain- To break my slender household chain,- Three pairs of little clasping hands, One voice, that whispers, not commands. Even while my spirit flies away, My gentle jailers murmur nay; All shapes of elemental wrath They raise along my threatened path; The storm grows black, the waters riso, The mountains mingle with the skies, The mad tornado scoops the ground, The midnight robber prowls around, - Thus, kissing every limb they tie, They draw a knot and heave a sigh, Till, fairly netted in the toil, My feet are rooted to the soil. Only the soaring wish is free!-- And that, dear Governor, flies to thee! }}
<section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />{{c|TO AN ENGLISH FRIEND}}
{{ppoem| THE seed that wasteful autumn cast To waver on its stormy blast, Long o'er the wintry desert tost, Its living germ has never lost. Dropped by the weary tempest's wing, It feels the kindling ray of spring, And, starting from its dream of death, Pours on the air its perfumed breath.
So, parted by the rolling flood, The love that springs from common blood Needs but a single sunlit honr Of mingling smiles to bud and flower; Unharmed its slumbering life has flown, From shore to shore, from zone to zone, Where summer's falling roses stain The tepid waves of Pontchartrain, Or where the lichen ereeps below Katahdin's wreaths of whirling snow.
Though fiery sun and stiffening cold May change the fair ancestral mould, No winter chills, no summer drains The life-blood drawn from English veins, Still bearing whereso'er it flows The love that with its fountain rose, Unchanged by space, unwronged by time, From age to age, from clime to clime! }}
<section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />{{c|AFTER A LECTURE ON WORDSWORTH}}
{{smaller block|[In 1853 Dr. Holmes gave a course of lectures before the Lowell Institute in Boston on English Poetry of the Nineteenth Century, and this and the following five poems were poatludes to the lectures.]}}
{{ppoem|end=follow| COME, spread your wings, as I spread mine, And leave the crowded hall For where the eyes of twilight shine O'er evening's western wall.
These are the pleasant Berkshire hills, Each with its leafy crown; Hark from their sides a thousand rilla Come singing sweetly down.
A thousand rills; they leap and shine, Strained through the shadowy nooks, Till, clasped in many a gathering twine, They swell a hundred brooks.
A hundred brooks, and still they run With ripple, shade, and gleam, Till, clustering all their braids in one, They flow a single stream.
A bracelet spun from mountain mist, A silvery sash unwound, With ox-bow curve and sinuous twist It writhes to reach the Sound.-
This is my bark, a pygmy's ship: Beneath a child it rolls; Fear not, one body makes it dip, But not a thousand souls.
Float we the grassy banks between; Without an oar we glide; The meadows, drest in living green, Unroll on either side.
Come, take the book we love so well, And let us read and dream We see whate'er its pages tell, And sail an English stream.
Up to the clouds the lark has sprung, Still trilling as he flies; }}<section end="s3" /><noinclude></noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|FAREWELL}}
{{c|{{smaller|TO J. R. LOWELL}}}}
{{center block|{{smaller block|[On the occasion of Lowell's going abroad in the spring of 1855.]}}}}
{{center block/s}} <poem> Farewell, for the bark has her breast to the tide, And the rough arms of Ocean are stretched for his bride; The winds from the mountain stream over the bay; One clasp of the had, then away and away!
I see the tall mast as it rocks by the shore; The sun is declining, I see it once more; To-day like the blade in a thick-waving field, To-morrow the spike on a Highlander's shield.
Alone, while the cloud pours its treacherous breath, With the blue lips all round her whose kisses are death; Ah, think not the breeze that is urging her sail Has left her unaided to strive with the gale.
There are hopes that play round her, like fires on the mast, That will light the dark hour till its danger has past; There are prayers that will plead with the storm when it raves, And whisper "Be still!" to the turbulent waves.
Nay, think not that Friendship has called us in vain To join the fair ring ere we break it again; There is strength in its circle,—you lose in the bright star, But its sisters still chain it, though shining afar.
I give you one health in the juice of the vine, The blood of the vineyard shall mingle with mine; Thus, let us drain the last dew-drops of gold, As we empty our hearts of the blessings they hold. </poem> {{center block/e}} <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />FOR THE MEETING GF THE BURNS CLUB 1856

When down their sides the crimson rills With mingled blood were flowing;

The raid that swooped with sword and
flame,
Give place to “law and order.”
Wot while the rocking steeples reel With midnight toesins ringing,
Not while the crashing war-notes peal, God sets his poets singing;
The bird is silent in the nicht, Or shucks a ery of warning
While fluttering round the beacon-light, — But hear him greet the morning t

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|FAREWELL}}

{{c|{{smaller|TO J. R. LOWELL}}}}

{{center block|{{smaller block|[On the occasion of Lowell's going abroad in the spring of 1855.]}}}}

{{ppoem|
Farewell, for the bark has her breast to the tide,
And the rough arms of Ocean are stretched for his bride;
The winds from the mountain stream over the bay;
One clasp of the had, then away and away!

I see the tall mast as it rocks by the shore;
The sun is declining, I see it once more;
To-day like the blade in a thick-waving field,
To-morrow the spike on a Highlander's shield.

Alone, while the cloud pours its treacherous breath,
With the blue lips all round her whose kisses are death;
Ah, think not the breeze that is urging her sail
Has left her unaided to strive with the gale.

There are hopes that play round her, like fires on the mast,
That will light the dark hour till its danger has past;
There are prayers that will plead with the storm when it raves,
And whisper "Be still!" to the turbulent waves.

Nay, think not that Friendship has called us in vain
To join the fair ring ere we break it again;
There is strength in its circle,—you lose in the bright star,
But its sisters still chain it, though shining afar.

I give you one health in the juice of the vine,
The blood of the vineyard shall mingle with mine;
Thus, let us drain the last dew-drops of gold,
As we empty our hearts of the blessings they hold.
}}

<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|FOR THE MEETING OF THE BURNS CLUB

1856}}}}

{{ppoem|
THE mountains glitter in the snow
A thousand leagues asunder;
Yet here, amid the banquet's glow,
I hear their voice of thunder;
Each giant's ice-bound goblet clinks;
A flowing stream is summoned;
Wachusett to Ben Nevis drinks;
Monadnock to Ben Lomond !
Though years have clipped the eagle's plume
That crowned the chieftain's bonnet,
The sun still sees the heather bloom,
The silver mists lio on it;
With tartan kilt and philibeg,
What stride was ever bolder
Than his who showed the naked leg
Beneath the plaided shoulder?
The echoes sleep on Cheriot's hills,
That heard the bugles blowing
When down their sides the crimson rills
With mingled blood were flowing;
The hunts where gallant hearts were game,
The slashing on the border,
The raid that swooped with sword and flame,
Give place to "law and order."
Not while the rocking steeples reel
With midnight tocsins ringing,
Not while the crashing war-notes peal,
God sets his poets singing;
The bird is silent in the night,
Or shricks a cry of warning
While fluttering round the beacon-light, -
But hear him greet the morning!
The lark of Scotia's morning sky!
Whose voice may sing his praises?
With Heaven's own sunlight in his eye,
He walked among the daisies,
Till through the cloud of fortune's wrong
He soared to fields of glory;
}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude></noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> But left bis land her sweetest song And earth her saddest story.
‘Tis mot the forts the builder piles That chain the earth together;
The wedded crowns, the sister isles, Would laugh at such a tether;
The kindling thought, the throbbing words, That set the pulses beating,
Are stronger than the myriad swords Of mighty armies meeting.
Thus while within the banquet glows, Without, the wild winds whistle, We drink a» triple health, —the Rose, The Shamrock, and the Thistle ! Their blended hues shall never fade "Fill War has hushed his cannon, — Close-iwined as oceau-eurreuts braid The ‘Fhames, the Clyde, the Shannon ! </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />ODE FOR WASHINGTON’S BIRTHDAY CELEBRATION OF THE MERCANTILE
LIBRARY ASSOCIATION, FEBRUARY 24, 1856
<poem> Welcome to the day returning, Dearer still as ages flow, While the torch of Faith is burning, Long as Freedom's altars glow! See the hero whom it gave us Slumbering on a mother's breast; For the arm he stretched to save us, Be its morn forever blest!
Hear the tale of youthful glory, While of Britain's rescued band Friend and foe repeat the story, Spread his fame o'er sea and land, Where the red cross, proudly streaming, Flaps above the frigate's deck, Where the golden lilies, gleaming, Star the watch-towers of Quebec.
Look! The shadow on the dial Marks the hour of deadlier strife; Days of terror, years of trial, Scourge a nation into life. Lo, the youth, become her leader! All her baffled tyrants yield; Through his arm the Lord hath freed her; Crown him on the tented field!
Vain is empire's mad temptation! Not for him an earthly crown! He whose sword hath freed a nation Strikes the offered sceptre down. See the throneless Conqueror seated, Ruler by a people's choice; See the Patriot's task completed; Hear the Father's dying voice!
"By the name that you inherit, By the sufferings you recall, Cherish the fraternal spirit; Love your country first of all! Listen not to idle questions If its bands may be untied; Doubt the patriot whose suggestions Strive a nation to divide!"
Father! We, whose ears have tingled With the discord-notes of shame,— We, whose sires their blood have mingled In the battle's thunder-flame,— Gathering, while this hold morning Lights the land from sea to sea, Hear thy counsel, heed thy warning; Trust us, while we honor thee! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />BIRTHDAY OF DANIEL WEB-
STEER JANUARY 18, 1836
<poem> Wen life hath run its largest raund Of toil and triumph, joy and woe,
How brief a storied page is fannd To compass all its ontward show !
The world-tried sailor tires and droops; His Hag is rent, his keel forgot;
Ilis farthest voyages seem lint loops That float from life’s entangled knot,
But when within the narrow space Sowe larger soul hath lived and wrought, Whose sicht was open to embrace The boundless realms of deed thought, —
and
When, stricken by the freezing blast, A nation’s living pillars fall,
How rich the storied page, how vast, A word, 4 whisper, can recall !
No medal lifts its fretted face, Nor speaking marble cheats your eye, </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude></noinclude>

And the last tottering pillars fall, Take the poor dust thy merey warms, Aad mould it into heavenly forms } </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />AT A BIRTHDAY FESTIVAL TO J. R. LOWELL FEBRUARY 22, 1859
<poem> We will not speak of years to-night,— For what have years to bring But larger floods of love and light, And sweeter songs to sing?
We will not drown in wordy praise The kindly thoughts that rise; If Friendship own one tender phrase, He reads it in our eyes.
We need not waste our school-boy art To gild this notch of Time;— Forgive me if my wayward heart Has throbbed in artless rhyme.
Enough for him the silent grasp That knits us hand in hand, And he the bracelet's radiant clasp That locks our circling band.
Strength to his hours of many toil! Peace to his starlit dreams! Who loves alike the furrowed soil, The music-haunted streams!
Sweet smiles to keep forever bright The sunshine on his lips, And faith that sees the ring of light Round nature's last eclipse! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />A BIRTHDAY TRIBUTE TO J. F. CLARKE, APRIL 4, 1860 <poem> Wao is the shepherd sent to lead,

sheep ?

To guide the fleck, or watch the fold;
True to all Truth the world denies, Not tongue-tied for its gilded sin;
Not always right in all men’s eyes, But faithful go the light within;
Who aske no meed of earthly fame, Who knows no earthly master’s call, Who hopes for man, through guilt and shame, Still answering, “ God is over all;”
Who makey another’s grief his own, Whose siile lends juy a double cheer; Where lives the saiut, if such be known 7—
Speak softly, —auch an one is here }

To thee our fragrant love we bring, In buds that April half displays,
Sweat first-born angels of the spring, Caught in their opening hymn of praise.
What though our faltering accents fail, Our captives know their message well,
Our words unbreathed their lips exhale, And sigh more loye than ours ean tell, </poem> <section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />THE GRAY Chinn

<poem> The noon of summer sheds its ray On Harvard's holy ground; The Matron calls, the sons obey, And gather smiling round.

Then old and young together stand, The sunshine and the snow, As heart to heart, and hand in hand, We sing before we go!
Her hundred opening doors have swung; Through every storied hall The pealing echoes loud have run, "Thrice welcome one and all!" The old and young, etc.
We floated though her peaceful bay, To sail life's stormy seas; But left our anchor where it lay Beneath her green old trees. The old and young, etc.
As now we lift its lengthening chain, That held us fast of old, The rusted rings grow bright again,— Their iron turns to gold. The old and young, etc.

{{c|{{larger|AT A MEETING OF FRIENDS}}}} {{c|{{smaller|AUGUST 29, 1859}}}} {{center block|{{smaller block|[The occasion was the fiftieth birthday of Dr. Holmes.]}}}} {{center block/s}} I remember — why, yes! God bless me! and was it so long ago?
I fear I'm growing forgetful, as old folks do, you know;
It must have been in 'forty — I would say 'thirty-nine —
We talked this matter over, I and a friend of mine. He said, "Well now, old fellow, I'm thinking that you and I,
If we act like other people, shall be older by and by;
What though the bright blue ocean is smooth as a pond can be,
There is always a line of breakers to fringe the broadest sea. "We're taking it mighty easy, but that is nothing strange,
For up to the age of thirty we spend our years like change;
But creeping up towards the forties, as fast as the old years fill,
And Time steps in for payment, we seem to change a bill." "I know it," I said, "old fellow; you speak the solemn truth;
A man can't live to a hundred and likewise keep his youth;
But what if the ten years coming shall silver-streak my hair,
You know I shall then be forty; of course I shall not care. "At forty a man grows heavy and tired of fun and noise;
Leaves dress to the five-and-twenties and love to the silly boys;
No foppish tricks at forty, no pinching of waists and toes,
But high-low shoes and flannels and good thick worsted hose." But one fine August morning I found myself awake:
My birthday: — By Jove, I'm forty! Yes forty and no mistake!
Why, this is the very milestone, I think I used to hold,
That when a fellow had come to, a fellow would then be old! But that is the young folks' nonsense; they're full of their foolish stuff;
A man's in his prime at forty, — I see ''that'' plain enough;
At ''fifty'' a man ''is'' wrinkled, and ''may be'' bald or gray;
I call men old at fifty, in spite of all they say. At last comes another August with mist and rain and shine;
Its mornings are slowly counted and creep to twenty-nine,
And when on the western summits the fading light appears,
It touches with rosy fingers the last of my fifty years. There have been both men and women whose hearts were firm and bold,
But there never was one of fifty that loved to say "I'm old;"
So any elderly person that strives to shirk his years,
Make him stand up at a table and try him by his peers. Now here I stand at fifty, my jury gathered round;
Sprinkled with dust of silver, but not yet silver-crowned,
Ready to meet your verdict, waiting to hear it told;
Guilty of fifty summers; speak! Is the verdict ''old?'' No! say that his hearing fails him; say that his sight grows dim;
Say that he's getting wrinkled and weak in back and limb,
Losing his wits and temper, but pleading, to make amends,
The youth of his fifty summers he finds in his twenty friends. {{center block/e}}

{{c|{{smaller|AUGUST 29, 1859}}}}

{{center block|{{smaller block|[The occasion was the fiftieth birthday of Dr. Holmes.]}}}}

{{ppoem|
{{sc|I remember}}—why, yes! God bless me! and was it so long ago?
I fear I'm growing forgetful, as old folks do, you know;
It must have been in 'forty—I would say 'thirty-nine—
We talked this matter over, I and a friend of mine.

He said, "Well now, old fellow, I'm thinking that you and I,
If we act like other people, shall be older by and by;
What though the bright blue ocean is smooth as a pond can be,
There is always a line of breakers to fringe the broadest sea.

"We're taking it mighty easy, but that is nothing strange,
For up to the age of thirty we spend our years like change;
But creeping up towards the forties, as fast as the old years fill,
And Time steps in for payment, we seem to change a bill."

"I know it," I said, "old fellow; you speak the solemn truth;
A man can't live to a hundred and likewise keep his youth;
But what if the ten years coming shall silver-streak my hair,
You know I shall then be forty; of course I shall not care.

"At forty a man grows heavy and tired of fun and noise;
Leaves dress to the five-and-twenties and love to the silly boys;
No foppish tricks at forty, no pinching of waists and toes,
But high-low shoes and flannels and good thick worsted hose."

But one fine August morning I found myself awake:
My birthday:—By Jove, I'm forty! Yes, forty and no mistake!
Why, this is the very milestone, I think I used to hold,
That when a fellow had come to, a fellow would then be old!

But that is the young folks' nonsense; they're full of their foolish stuff;
A man's in his prime at forty,—I see ''that'' plain enough;
At ''fifty'' a man ''is'' wrinkled, and ''may be'' bald or gray;
I call men old at fifty, in spite of all they say.

At last comes another August with mist and rain and shine;
Its mornings are slowly counted and creep to twenty-nine,
And when on the western summits the fading light appears,
It touches with rosy fingers the last of my fifty years.

There have been both men and women whose hearts were firm and bold,
But there never was one of fifty that loved to say "I'm old;"
So any elderly person that strives to shirk his years,
Make him stand up at a table and try him by his peers.

Now here I stand at fifty, my jury gathered round;
Sprinkled with dust of silver, but not yet silver-crowned,
Ready to meet your verdict, waiting to hear it told;
Guilty of fifty summers; speak! Is the verdict ''old?''

No! say that his hearing fails him; say that his sight grows dim;
Say that he's getting wrinkled and weak in back and limb,
Losing his wits and temper, but pleading, to make amends,
The youth of his fifty summers he finds in his twenty friends.

<section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />INTERNATIONAL ODE
QUR PATHERS’ LAND
This ode was sung in unison by twelve hun- dred children of the public schools to the air of “God save the Queen '' at the visit of the Prince of Wales to Boston, October 18, 1860,
<poem> God bless our Fathers' Land! Keep her in heart and hand One with our own! From all her foes defend, Be her brave People's Friend, On all her realms descend, Protect her Throne!
Father, with loving car Guard Thou her kingdom's Heir, Guide all his ways: Thine arm his shelter be, From him by land and sea Bid storm and danger flee, Prolong his days!
Lord, let War's tempest cease, Fold the whole Earth in peace Under thy wings! Make all thy nations one, All hearts beneath the sun, Till Thou shalt reign alone, Great King of kings! </poem>

LT have walked ke a laml by the friend, by the friend, That stuck ta my skirts like a bur; Thave borne the stale talk without end, withont ond, OF the sitter whom nothing could stir:
But my hamstrings grow loose, and I shake, and [ shake, At the sight of the dreadfnl Old Man; Yea, I quiver and quake, and I take, and I tuke To my legs with what vigor I can |
Oh the dreadful Old Man of the Sea, of the Sea }
He‘s come back like the Wandering Jew!
He bas had his cold claw upon me, upon
me, — And be sure that he ‘ll have it on you! </poem>
<section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />INTERNATIONAL ODE
OUR FATHERS’ LAND
This ode was sung in unison by twelve hun- dred children of the public schools to the air of “God save the Queen” at the visit of the Prince of Wales to Boston, October 18, 1860,
<poem> God bless our Fathers' Land! Keep her in heart and hand One with our own! From all her foes defend, Be her brave People's Friend, On all her realms descend, Protect her Throne!
Father, with loving car Guard Thou her kingdom's Heir, Guide all his ways: Thine arm his shelter be, From him by land and sea Bid storm and danger flee, Prolong his days!
Lord, let War's tempest cease, Fold the whole Earth in peace Under thy wings! Make all thy nations one, All hearts beneath the sun, Till Thou shalt reign alone, Great King of kings! </poem>
<section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />VIVE LA FRANCE
A SENTIMENT OFFERED AT THE DINNER TO H, 1, H. THE PRINCE NAPOLEON, AT THE REVERE HOUSE, SEPTEMBER 25, 1861 <poem> Tue land of sunshine and of song! [ley name your hearts divine; To her the banquet’s vows belong Whose breasts have poured its wine; Our trusty friend, our true ally Through varied change and chances So, fill your flashing goblets high, — I give you, Vivn is France! </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude></noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" /></noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> Let it pass with a plass Fer the Cass or 729."
As one by ane is falling Beneath the leaves or snows, Each memory still recalling, The broken ring shall close, Till the nightwinds softly pass Oer the green and growing grass, Where it waves on the grayes = Of the Boys or “291 </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Las5z <poem> Where, oh where are the visions of morning, Fresh as the dews of our prime? Gone, like tenants that quit without warning, Down the back entry of time.
Where, oh where are life's lilies and roses, Nursed in the golden dawn's smile? Dead as the bulrushes round little Moses, On the old banks of the Nile.
Where are the Marys, and Anns, and Elizas, Loving and lovely of yore? Look in the columns of old Advertisers,— Married and dead by the score.
Where the gray colts and the ten-year-old fillies, Saturday's triumph and joy? Gone, like our friend πόὂας ὠκὺς Achilles, [[Author:Homer|Homer]]'s ferocious old boy.
Die-away dreams of ecstatic emotion, Hopes like young eagles at play, Vows of unheard-of and endless devotion, How ye have faded away!
Yet, though the ebbing of Time's might river Leave our young blossoms to die, Let him roll smooth in his current forever, Til the last pebble is dry. </poem>

Who asks if his comrade is battered and tanned
When he feels his warm soul in the clasp of his hand %
No ! be it an epic, or be if a line,
The Boys will all love ib because tf is mine;
I suug their last song on the morn of the day
‘That tore from their lives the last blossom of May.
Jt is not the sunset that glows in the wine,
But the smile that beams aver it, makes it divine;
I seatter these drops, and behold, as they fall,
The day-star of memory shines through them all |
And these are the last; they are drops that I stole
From a wine-press that ernshes the life from the soul,
But they ran through my heart and they aprang to my brain
Till our twentieth sweet summer was smil- ing apain | </poem> <section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />THE OLD MAN DREAMS

Will Earth to pagan dreams return To find from misery’s pamted urn That all save hope bas flown, — Of Book and Church and Priest bereft, The Rovk of Ages yaiuly cleft, Life’s compass gone, its auchor left, Left, — lost, — in depths unknown ? Shail Fuith the trodden path pursue, . The crux ansaia wearers knew Wha sleep with folded hands, Where, like a naked, lidless eye, The staring Nile rolls wandering by Those mountain slopes that climb the sky Above the drifting sands ? Or shall a nobler Faith return, Nts fanes a purer gospel learn, With holier anthems ring, And teach us that our transient creeds Were but the perishable seeds Of haryests sown for larger needs, That ripening years shall bring ? Well, let the present do its best, We trast our Maker for the reat, As on our way we plod; Qur sonis, full dressed in fleshly suits, Love air and sunshine, flowers and fruits, The duisies better than their roots Beneath the grassy sod. Not bed-time yet ! The full-blown flower Of all the year — this evening hour — With friendship’s flame is bright; Life still is sweet, the heavens are fair, Though fields are brown and woods are hare, And many a joy is left to share Before wa say Good-night ! And when, our cheerful evening past, The nurse, long waiting, comes at leat, Ere on her lap we lie In wearied nature's sweet repose, At peace with all her waking foes, Our lips shall murmuz, ere they close, Good-night ! and not Good-by !
A LOVING-CUP SONG 1883 Comm, heap the fagots! Ere we go Again the cheerful hearth shall glow; 148 We ‘Il have another blaze, my boys! When clouds are black and snows are white, Then Christinas logs lend ruddy light They stole from summer days, my boya, They stole from summer days. And let the Loving-Cup go round, The Cup with blessed memories crowned, That Hows whene’er we meet, my boys; No draught will hold a drop of ain If love ia only well ativred in To keep it sound and sweet, my boys, To keep it sound and sweet. Give me, to pin upon my bresst, The blossoms twain I love the best, A rosebud and a pink, my boys: Their leaves shall nestle next my heart, Their perfumed breath shall own its part In every health we drink, my boys, In every health we drink. The breathing blossoms stir my bleod, Methinks I see the lilacs bad And hear the blucbirds sing, my boys; Why not? Yon lusty oak has seen Full tenscore years, yet leaflets green Peep ont with every spring, my boys, Peep out with every spring, Old Time his rusty scythe may whet, The umnowed grass is glowing yet Beneath the sheltering snew, my boys; And if the erazy dotard ask, Is lave worn out? Is life a task 7 We ‘ll bravely answer No! my boys, We'll bravely answer No ! For life’s bright taper is the same Lave tipped of old with resy flame That heaven’s own altay leut, my beys, To glow in every cup we fill Till lips are mute and hearts ave still, Till life and love are spent, my boys, ‘Vill life and love are spent.
THE GIRDLE OF FRIENDSHIP 1884. She gathered at her slender waist The beauteous robe she wore; Its folds a golden belt embraced, One rose-hued gem it bore.

revision.text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> The girdle shrank; its lessening round Still kept the shining gem, But now her flowing locks it bound, A lustrous diadem.
And narrower still the circlet grew; Behold! a glittering band, Its roseate diamond set anew, Her neck's white column spanned.
Suns rise and set; the straining clasp The shortened links resist, Yet flashes in a bracelet's grasp The diamond, on her wrist.
At length, the round of changes past The thieving years could bring, The jewel, glittering to the last, Still sparkles in a ring.
So, link by link, our friendships part, So loosen, break, and fall, A narrowing zone; the loving heart Lives changeless through them all. </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />THE LYRE OF ANACREON 1885 <poem> Tue minstref of the classic lay Of love and wine who sings Still found the fingers run astray
That touched the rebel strings.
Of Cadmus he would fain have sung, OF Atreus and his line;
But all the jocund echoes rung With soups of love anid wine.
Ah, brothers |! I would fain have caught Some fresher fancy’s gleam;
My truant aecents find, unsought, The old familiar theme.
Love, Love! but not the sportive child With shaft and twanging bow,
Whose random arrows drove us wild Some threeseore years ago:
Not Eros, with his joyous laugh, The urchin blind and bare,
But Love, with spectacles and staff, And geanty, silvered hutr.
Our heads with frosted locks are white, Qur reofs are thatched with snow, But ved, in chilling winter's spite, Oar hearts and hearthstones glow.
Our old acquaintance, Time, drops in, And while the running sands
Their golden thread unheeded spin, He warms his frozen hands,
Stay, wingéd hours, too swift, too sweet, And watt this message o’er
To all we miss, from all we meet On life's fest-crumbling shore:
Say that, to old affection true, We hug the narrowing chain
That binds our hearts, — ales, how few The links that yet remain !
The fatal toueh awaits them all ‘That furns the rocks to dust;
From year te year they break and fail, — They break, but never rust.
Say if one note of happier strain ‘This worn-cut harp afferd, —
One throb that trembles, not in vain, — Their memory lent its chord.
Say that when Faney closed her wings Aud Passion quenched his fire,
Love, Love, still echoed from the strings As from Anacreon’s lyre ! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />THE OLD TUNE THIRTY-SIXTH VARIATION
1886 <poem> Tris shred of song you bid me bring Is snatehed from faney's embers;
Ah, when the lips forget to sing, The faithful heart remembers !
Too swift the wings of envious Time To wait for dallymg phrases,
Or woven strands of labored rhyme To thread their cunning mazes.
A word, a sigh, and lo, how plain Tis magic breath discloses
Our life’s long vista through a lane Of threescore summiers’ roses ! </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> We track his footsteps, but we never find
him: Stroug locks are broken, massive bolta are drawn,
And all around are left the bars and borers, The xplitling wedges and the prying
keys, Such aids as serve the soft-shod vault-ex- plorers To crack, wrench open, rifle as they please.
Ah, these ave tools which Heaven in meroy lends us t When enthermg rust has clenched our shackles fast, Time is the angel-thief that Nature sends us Yo break the cramping fetters of our past,
Mourn as we may for treasures he has tuken, Poor as we feel of hoarded wealth bereft,
Bore precious sre those implements for- |
saken, Found in the wreck his ruthless hands have left.
Some lever that a casket’s hinge has broken Pries off a bolt, and le! cur souls are free; Each year some Open Sesame is spekon, And every decade drops its master-key,
So us from year to year we count our treas- ure, Our loss seems les¢, and larger look onr gains; Tisne’s wrongs repaid in more than even weasure, — We lose our jewels, but we break our chains. </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />AFTER THE CURFEW 1889
[Fhe only remaining meeting of the class at Parker's was in 1890, three present. There was no poem. |
<poem> The Play is over. While the light Yet lingers in the darkening hall, I come to say a last Good-night Before the final ''Exeunt all''.
We gathered once, a joyous throng; The jovial toasts went gaily round; With jest, and laugh, and shout, and song, We made the floors and walls resound.
We come with feeble steps and slow, A little band of four or five, Left from the wrecks of long ago, Still pleased to find ourselves alive.
Alive! How living, too, are they Whose memories it is ours to share! Spread the long table's full array,— There sits a ghost in every chair!
One breathing form no more, alas! Amid our slender group we see; With him we still remained "The Class,"— Without his presence what are we?
The hand we ever loved to clasp,— That tireless hand which knew no rest,— Loosed from affection's clinging grasp, Lies nerveless on the peaceful breast.
The beaming eye, the cheering voice, That lent to life a generous glow, Whose every meaning said, "Rejoice," We see, we hear, no more below.
The air seems darkened by his loss, Earth's shadowed features look less fair, And heavier weights the daily cross His willing shoulders helped us bear.
Why mourn that we, the favored few Whom grasping Time so long has spared Life's sweet illusions to pursue, The common lot of age have shared?
In every pulse of Friendship's heart There breeds unfelt a throb of pain,— One hour must rend its links apart, Though years on years have forged the chain.
So ends "The Boys," — a lifelong play. We too must hear the Prompter's call To fairer scenes and brighter day: Farewell! I let the curtain fall. </poem><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{rh|148|POEMS OF THE CLASS OF '29}} {{rule}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{ppoem|start=follow| We track his footsteps, but we never find bim: Strong locks are broken, massive bolts are drawn, And all around are left the bars and borers, The splitting wedges and the prying keys, I come to say a last Good-night Before the final Exeunt all. We gathered once, a joyous throng: The jovial toasts went gayly round; With jest, and laugh, and shout, and song, We made the floors and walls resound. We come with feeble steps and slow, A little band of four or five, Such aids as serve the soft-shod vault-explurcs To crack, wrench open, rifle as they Left from the wrecks of long ago, please. Ah, these are tools which Heaven in mercy lends us! When gathering rust has elenched our shackles fast, Time is the angel-thief that Nature sends us To break the cramping fetters of our past. Mourn as we may for treasures he has tuken, Poor as we feel of hoarded wealth bereft, More precious are those implements for saken, Found in the wreck his ruthless hands have left. Some lever that a casket's hinge has broken Pries off a bolt, and lu! our souls are free; Each year some Open Sesame is spoken, And every decade drops its master-key. So as from year to year we count our treasure, Our loss seems less, and larger look our gains; Tine's wrongs repaid in more than even measure,- We lose our jewels, but we break our chains. }}
<section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />{{c|AFTER THE CURFEW
1889}}
{{center block|{{smaller block|[The only remaining meeting of the class at Parker's was in 1890, three present. There was no poem.]}}
{{ppoem| THE Play is over. While the light Yet lingers in the darkening hall, Still pleased to find ourselves alive. Alive! How living, too, are they Whose memories it is ours to share! Spread the long table's full array,- There sits a ghost in every chair! One breathing form no more, alas ! Amid our slender group we see; With him we still remained "The Class,". Without his presence what are we? The hand we ever loved to clasp, -- That tireless band which knew no rest,- Loosed from affection's clinging grasp, Lies nerveless on the peaceful breast. The beaming eye, the cheering voice, That lent to life a generous glow, Whose every meaning said "Rejoice," We see, we hear, no more below. The air seems darkened by his loss, Earth's shadowed features look less fair, And heavier weighs the daily cross His willing shoulders helped us bear, Why mourn that we, the favored few Whom grasping Time so long has spared Life's sweet illusions to pursue, The common lot of age have shared? In every pulse of Friendship's heart There breeds unfelt a throb of pain,- One hour must rend its links apart, Though years on years have forged the chain. - So ends "The Boys," a lifelong play. We too must hear the Prompter's call To fairer scenes and brighter day: Farewell! I let the curtain fall. }}<section end="s2" /><noinclude></noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />POEMS FROM THE PROFESSOR AT THE BREAKFAST- TABLE
1858-1859 <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />UNDER THE VIOLETS
<poem> Her hands are cold; her face is white; No more her pulse come and go; Her eyes are shut to life and light;— Fold the white vesture, snow on snow, And lay her where the violets blow.
But not beneath a graven stone, To plead for tears with alien eyes; A slender cross of wood alone Shall say, that here a maiden lies In peace beneath the peaceful skies.
And gray old trees of hugest limb Shall wheel their circling shadows round To make the scorching sunlight dim That drinks the greenness from the ground, And drop their dead leaves on her mound.
When o'er their boughs the squirrels run, And through their leaves the robins call, And, ripening in the autumn sun, The acorns and the chestnuts fall, Doubt not that she will heed them all.
For her the morning choir shall sing Its matins from the branches high, And every minstrel-voice of Spring, That trills beneath the April sky, Shall greet her with its earliest cry.
When, turning round their dial-track, Eastward the lengthening shadows pass, Her little mourners, clad in black, The crickets, sliding through the grass, Shall pipe for her an evening mass.
At last the rootlets of the trees Shall find the prison where she lies, And bear the buried dust they seize In leaves and blossoms to the skies. So may the soul that warmed it rise!
If any, born of kindlier blood, Should ask, What maiden lies below? Say only this: A tender bud, That tried to blossom in the snow, Lies withered where the violets blow. </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />HYMN OF TRUST <poem> O Love Divine, that stooped ta share Our sharpest pang, our bitterest tear,
On Thee we east each earth-born pare, We smile at pain while Thou art near !
Thongh long the weary way we tread, And sorrow crown each lingermg year, No path wa shun, no darkness dread, Our hearts still whispering, Thou art near |
When drooping pleasure terns to grief, And trembling faith is changed to fear,
The murmuring wind, the quivering leaf, Shall softly tell us, Thou art near !
On Thea we fling our burdening woe, O Love Divine, forever dear,
Content te suffer while we know, Living and dying, Thou art near t </poem> <section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />A SUN-DAY HYMN <poem> Lorp of all being | throned afar, Thy glory flames from sua end star 4 Centre and soul of every sphere,
Yet te each loving heart how near ! </poem><section end="s4" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

Her eyes are shut to life and light;—

A slender cross of wood alone
{{em}}Shall say, that here a maiden lies
{{em}}In peace beneath the peaceful skies. And gray old trees of hugest limb

{{em}}That drinks the greenness from the ground,

<section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />{{c|HYMN OF TRUST}}
{{ppoem| {{sc|O Love}} Divine, that stooped to share {{em}}Our sharpest pang, our bitterest tear, On Thee we cast each earth-born care, {{em}}We smile at pain while Thou art near!
Though long the weary way we tread, {{em}}And sorrow crown each lingering year, No path we shun, no darkness dread, {{em}}Our hearts still whispering, Thou art near!
When drooping pleasure turns to grief, {{em}}And trembling faith is changed to fear, The murmuring wind, the quivering leaf, {{em}}Shall softly tell us, Thou art near!
On Thee we fling our burdening woe, {{em}}O Love Divine, forever dear, Content to suffer while we know, {{em}}Living and dying, Thou art near! }}
<section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />{{c|A SUN-DAY HYMN}}
{{ppoem|end=stanza| {{sc|Lord}} of all being! throned afar, Thy glory flames from sun and star; Centre and soul of every sphere, Yet to each loving heart how near! }}<section end="s4" /><noinclude></noinclude>

Our midnight is thy smile withdrawn; Our noontide is thy gracious dawn; Our rainbow arch thy mercy's sign; All, save the clouds of sin, are thine!
Lord of all life, below, above, Whose light is truth, whose warmth is love, Before thy ever-blazing throne We ask no lustre of our own.
Grant us thy truth to make us free, And kindling hearts that burn for thee, Till all thy living altars claim One holy light, one heavenly flame!}} {{dhr}} <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />{{c|THE CROOKED FOOTPATH}}
{{ppoem|{{sc|Ah}}, here it is! the sliding rail {{em}}That marks the old remembered spot,— The gap that struck our school-boy trail,— {{em}}The crooked path across the lot.
It left the road by school and church, {{em}}A pencilled shadow, nothing more, That parted from the silver-birch {{em}}And ended at the farm-house door.
No line or compass traced its plan; {{em}}With frequent bends to left or right, In aimless, wayward curves it ran, {{em}}But always kept the door in sight.
The gabled porch, with woodbine green,— {{em}}The broken millstone at the sill,— Though many a rood might stretch between, {{em}}The truant child could see them still.
No rocks across the pathway lie,— {{em}}No fallen trunk is o'er it thrown,— And yet it winds, we know not why, {{em}}And turns as if for tree or stone.
Perhaps some lover trod the way {{em}}With shaking knees and leaping heart,— And so it often runs astray {{em}}With sinuous sweep or sudden start.
Or one, perchance, with clouded brain {{em}}From some unholy banquet reeled,— And since, our devious steps maintain {{em}}His track across the trodden field.
Nay, deem not thus,—no earthborn will {{em}}Could ever truce a faultless line; Our truest steps are human still,— {{em}}To walk unswerving were divine!
Truants from love, we dream of wrath;— {{em}}Oh, rather let us trust the more! Through all the wanderings of the path {{em}}We still can see our Father's door!}} {{dhr}} <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />{{c|IRIS, HER BOOK}}
{{sc|I Pray}} thee by the soul of her that bore thee, By thine own sister's spirit I implore thee, Deal gently with the leaves that lie before thee!
For Iris had no mother to infold her, Nor ever leaned upon a sister's shoulder, Telling the twilight thoughts that Nature told her.
She had not learned the mystery of awaking Those chorded keys that soothe a sorrow's aching, Giving the dumb heart voice, that else were breaking.
Yet lived, wrought, suffered. Lo, the pictured token! Why should her fleeting day-dreams fade unspoken, Like daffodils that die with sheaths unbroken?
She knew not love, yet lived in maiden fancies,— Walked simply clad, a queen of high romances, And talked strange tongues with angels in her trances,
Twin-souled she seemed, a twofold nature wearing: Sometimes a flashing falcon in her daring, Then a poor mateless dove that droops despairing.}}<section end="s3" /><noinclude></noinclude>

{{rvh|164|FROM THE PROFESSOR AT THE BREAKFAST-TABLE}} {{center block/s}}
Sun of our life, thy quickening ray
Sheds on our path the glow of day;
Star of our hope, thy softened light
Cheers the long watches of the night. Our midnight is thy smile withdrawn;
Our noontide is thy gracious dawn;
Our rainbow arch thy mercy's sign;
All, save the clouds of sin, are thine! Lord of all life, below, above,
Whose light is truth, whose warmth is love,
Before thy ever-blazing throne
We ask no lustre of our own. Grant us thy truth to make us free,
And kindling hearts that burn for thee,
Till all thy living altars claim
One holy light, one heavenly flame! {{center block/e}}
{{c|THE CROOKED FOOTPATH}} {{center block/s}} {{sc|Ah}}, here it is! the sliding rail
{{em}}That marks the old remembered spot,—
The gap that struck our school-boy trail,—
{{em}}The crooked path across the lot. It left the road by school and church,
{{em}}A pencilled shadow, nothing more,
That parted from the silver-birch
{{em}}And ended at the farm-house door. No line or compass traced its plan;
{{em}}With frequent bends to left or right,
In aimless, wayward curves it ran,
{{em}}But always kept the door in sight. The gabled porch, with woodbine green,—
{{em}}The broken millstone at the sill,—
Though many a rood might stretch between,
{{em}}The truant child could see them still. No rocks across the pathway lie,—
{{em}}No fallen trunk is o'er it thrown,—
And yet it winds, we know not why,
{{em}}And turns as if for tree or stone. Perhaps some lover trod the way
{{em}}With shaking knees and leaping heart,—
And so it often runs astray
{{em}}With sinuous sweep or sudden start. Or one, perchance, with clouded brain
{{em}}From some unholy banquet reeled,—
And since, our devious steps maintain
{{em}}His track across the trodden field. Nay, deem not thus,—no earthborn will
{{em}}Could ever truce a faultless line;
Our truest steps are human still,—
{{em}}To walk unswerving were divine! Truants from love, we dream of wrath;—
{{em}}Oh, rather let us trust the more!
Through all the wanderings of the path
{{em}}We still can see our Father's door! {{center block/e}} ## s3 ##
{{c|IRIS, HER BOOK}} {{center block/s}} {{sc|I Pray}} thee by the soul of her that bore thee,
By thine own sister's spirit I implore thee,
Deal gently with the leaves that lie before thee! For Iris had no mother to infold her,
Nor ever leaned upon a sister's shoulder,
Telling the twilight thoughts that Nature told her. She had not learned the mystery of awaking
Those chorded keys that soothe a sorrow's aching,
Giving the dumb heart voice, that else were breaking. Yet lived, wrought, suffered. Lo, the pictured token!
Why should her fleeting day-dreams fade unspoken,
Like daffodils that die with sheaths unbroken? She knew not love, yet lived in maiden fancies,—
Walked simply clad, a queen of high romances,
And talked strange tongues with angels in her trances, Twin-souled she seemed, a twofold nature wearing:
Sometimes a flashing falcon in her daring,
Then a poor mateless dove that droops despairing. {{nop}}
{{center block/e}}

<poem> Thus I lift the sash, so long Shut against the flight of song; All too late for vain excuse,— Lo, my captive rhymes are loose!
Rhymes that, flitting through my brain, Beat against my window-pane, Some with gayly colored wings, Some, alas! with venomed stings.
Shall they bask in sunny rays? Shall they feed on sugared praise? Shall they stick with tangled feet On the critic's poisoned sheet?
Are the outside winds too rough? Is the world not wide enough? Go, my wingèd verse, and try,— Go, like Uncle Toby's fly! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />PROGRAMME
OCTOBER 7, 1874 <poem> Reaprr — gentle — if so be Such still live, aud live for me, Will it please you to be told What my tenseore pages held 7
Here are verses that in spite Of myself I needs must write, Like the wine that oozes first
When the unsqueezed grapes have burst.
Here are angry lines, ‘too hard!” Says the soldier, battle-searred. Could I amile his sears away
J would blot the intter lay,
Written with a knitted brow, Read with placid wonder now.
Throbbed such passion in my heart ? Did his wounds once really smart ?
Here are varied strains that sing All the chauyes life can bring, Songs when joyous friends hare met, Songs the mourner's tears have wet.
See the banquet’s dead bonquet, Fair and iragrant in its day;
De they read the selfsame lines, — He that fusts und he that dines ?
Year by year, like milestones placed, Mark the reeurd Friendship traced, Priseued in the walls of time
Life has notched ifself in rhyme:
As its seasons slid along,
Every yeur a notch of song, From the June of long ago, Wheu the rose was full in blow,
Till the searlet sage has come And tha sold chrysanthemum. Read, but not to praise or blame} Are not all our hearts the same 7
For the rast, they take their chance, — Some may pay a passing glance; Others, — well, they served a turn, — Wherefore written, would you learn 7
Noé for glory, not for pelf,
Not, be sure, to please myself, Not for any meaner ends, — Always “by request of friends.”
Here’s the consin of a king, — Would I do the civil thing 7 Here ’s the first-born of a queen: Here ’s 2 slant-eyed Mandarin. </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

But it involved a principle of taxation. to which the Uoluniss would not submit. ‘Their objection way uot te the amuunt, but the elains. The Mast Indian Company, however, sent out a number ot tea-ships to different American ports, three of them te Boston.

Read at a meeting of the Massachusetts His- torieal Society in L874.
<poem> No! never such a draught was poured Since Hebe served with nectar The bright Olympians and their Lord, Her over-kind protector,— Since Father Noah squeezed the grape And took to such behaving As would have shamed our grandsire ape Before the days of shaving,— No! ne'er was mingled such a draught In palace, hall, or arbor, As freemen brewed and tyrants quaffed That night in Boston Harbor! It kept King George so long awake His brain at last got addled, It made the nerves of Britain shake, With sevenscore millions saddled; Before that bitter cup was drained, Amid the roar of cannon, The Western war-cloud's crimson stained The Thames, the Clyde, the Shannon; Full many a six-foot grenadier The flattened grass had measured, And many a mother many a year Her tearful memories treasured; Fast spread the tempest's darkening pall, The storm broke loose, but first of all The Boston teapot bubbled!
An evening party,—only that, No formal invitation, No gold-laced coat, no stiff cravat, No feast in contemplation, No silk-robed dames, no fiddling band, No flowers, no songs, no dancing,— A tribe of red men, axe in hand,— Behold the guests advancing! What a glimpse Of paint and fur and feather, As all at once the full-grown imps Light on the deck together! <noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|A BALLAD OF THE BOSTON TEA-PARTY}}
The tax on tea, which was considered so odious and led to the act on which ''A Ballad of the Boston Tea Party'' is founded, was but a small matter, only twopence in the pound. But it involved a principle of taxation. to which the Colunies would not submit. Their objection was not to the amount, but the claim. The East Indian Company, however, sent out a number ot tea-ships to different American ports, three of them to Boston.
The inhabitants tried to send them back, but in vain. The captains of the ships had consented, if permitted, to return with their cargoes to England, but the consignees refused to dischare them from their obligations, the custom house to give them a clearance for their return, and the governor to grant them a passport for gulug by the fort. It was easily seen that the tea would be gradually landed from the ships lying so near the town, and that if landed it would be disposed of, and the purpose of establishing the monopoly and raising a revenue effected. To prevent the dreaded consequence, a number of armed men, disguised like Indians, boarded the ships and threw their whole cargoes of tea into the dock. About seventeen persons boarded the ships in Boston harbor, and emptied three hundred and forty-two chests of tea. Among these "Indians" was Major Thomas Melville, the same who supgestad to me the poem, ''The Last Leaf''.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> O woman, at the evening board So gracious, sweet, and purring, So happy while the tea is poured, So blest while spoons are stirring, What martyr can compare with thee, The mother, wife, or daughter, That night, instead of best Bohea, Condemned to milk and water!
Ah, little dreams the quiet dame Who plies with rock and spindle The patient flax, how great a flame You little spark shall kindle! The lurid morning shall reveal A fire no king can smother Where British flint and Boston steel Have clashed against each other! Old charters shrivel in its track, His Worship's bench has crumbled, It climbs and clasps the union-jack, Its blazoned pomp is humbled, The flags go down on land and sea Like corn before the reapers; So burned the fire that brewed the tea That Boston served her keepers!
The waves that wrought a century's wreck Have rolled o'er whig and tory; The Mohawks on the Dartmouth's deck Still live in song and story; The waters in the rebel bay Have kept the tea-leaf savor; Our old North-Enders in their spray Still taste a Hyson flavor; And Freedom's teacup still o'erflows With ever fresh libations, To cheat of slumber all her foes And cheer the wakening nations! </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />NEARING THE SNOW-LINE

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> You whom the fathers made free and defended, Stain not the scroll that emblazons their fame! You whose fair heritage spotless descended, Leave not your children a birthright of shame!
Stay not for questions while Freedom stands gasping! Wait not till Honor lies wrapped in his pall! Brief the lips' meeting be, swift the hands' clasping,— "Off for the wars!" is enough for them all!
Break from the arms that would fondly caress you! Hark! 'tis the bugle-blast, sabres are drawn! Mothers shall pray for you, fathers shall bless you, Maidens shall weep for you when you are gone!
Never or now! cries the blood of a nation, Poured on the turf where the red rose should bloom; Now is the day and the hour of salvation,— Never or now! peals the trumpet of doom!
Never or now! roars the hoarse-throated cannon Through the black canopy blotting the skies; Never or now! flaps the shell-blasted pennon O'er the deep ooze where the Cumberland lies!
From the foul dens where our brothers are dying, Aliens and foes in the land of their birth,— From the rank swamps where our martyrs are lying Pleading in vain for a handful of earth,—
From the hot plains where they perish outnumbered, Furrowed and ridged by the battle-field's plough, Comes the loud summons; too long you have slumbered, Hear the last Angel-trump,—Never or Now! </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />ILY MN
WRITTEN FOR THE GREAT CENTRAL FAIR EN PHILADELPHIA, 1564
[This hynm was to have been sung at the Inaugural Ceremonies June 7, but an accident to the singers’ platform: prevented its use in that form. | <poem> PATHER, send on Earth again
Pease und pood-will to mex;
Yet, while the weary track of life
Leuds thy peuple through storm and atrifa, Help us to walk therein,
Guide us through the perilons path; Teach us love that tempers wrath; Let the fountain of merey flaw Alike for helpless friend and foe, Children all of Thine.
God of grace, hear our call;
Bless our gifts, Giver of all;
The wounded heal, the captive restore, And make us a nation evermore Faithful to Freedom and Thee, </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />ONE COUNTRY 1865 <poem> One country! Treason’s writhing asp Struck madly at her girdle’s clasp, And Hatred wrenched with might and main To rend its welded links in twain, While Mammon hugged his golden calf Content to take one broken half, While thankless churls stood idly by And heard unmoved a nation’s cry $
One country! “ Nay,” —the tyrant crew
Shrieked from their dens, —“it shall be two l
Til bodes te us this monstrous birth,
That scowls on all the thrones of earth,
Too broad yon starry cluster shines,
Too proudly tower the New-World pines,
Tear down the ‘banner of the free,’
And cleave their and from sea to sea!” </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

1865 <poem> Grver of all that crowne our days,
With grateful hearts we sing thy praise; Through deep and desert led by Thee, Our promised lund at last we see,
Ruler of Nations, judge our cause |
LE we have kept thy holy laws,
The sons of Belial curse in vain
The day that rends the captive’s chain.
Thou God of vengeance! Isracl’s Lord! Break in their grasp the shield and sword, And make thy righteous judgments kuowr Till all thy foes are overthrown !
Then, Father, lay thy healing hand Lu mercy on our stricken laud; Lead all its wanderers to the fold, And be their Shepherd as af oli.
So shall one Nation’s song ascend
To Thee, our Ruler, Father, Friend, While Heayen’s wide arch resounds agair With Peace on earth, good-will to men ! </poem> <section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />HYMN FOR THE FAIR AT CHICAGO 1865 <poem> © Gop! in danger’s darkest hour, In battle’s deadliest field,
Thy name has been our Nation’s tower, Ty truth her help and shield.
Our lips shanld fill the air with praise, Nor pay the debt we owe,
So high above the songs we raise The floods of mercy How.
Yet Thon wilt hear the prayer we speak, The song of praise we sing, —
Thy children, who thine altar seek Their grateful gifts to bring. </poem><section end="s4" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> Fear Het for hii, though the rebels expect un, — Life iz too preeious to shorten ita span; Wouan her broomstick shall raise to pro- teet him, Will she not fight for the sweet little man ?
Now then, nine cheers for the Stay-at-Home Ranger! Blow the great fish-horn and beat the big pan! First im the field that is farthest from danger, Take your white-feather plume, sweet little man | </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />UNION AND LIBERTY
<poem> Flag of the heroes who left us their glory, Borne through their battle-fields' thunder and flame, Blazoned in song and illumined in story, Wave o'er us all who inherit their fame! Up with our banner bright, Sprinkled with starry light, Spread its fair emblems from mountain to shore, While through the sounding sky Loud rings the Nation's cry,— {{sc|Union and Liberty! One evermore!}}
Light of our firmament, guide of our Nation, Pride of her children, and honored afar, Let the wide beams of thy full constellation Scatter each cloud that would darken a star! Up with our banner bright, etc.
Empire unsceptred! what foe shall assail thee, Bearing the standard of Liberty's van? Think not the God of thy fathers shall fail thee, Striving with men for the birthright of man! Up with our banner bright, etc.
Yes if, by madness and treachery blighted, Dawns the dark hour when the sword thou must draw, Then with the arms of thy millions united, Smite the bold traitors to Freedom and Law! Up with our banner bright, etc.
Lord of the Universe! shield us and guide us, Trusting Thee always, through shadow and sun! Thou hast united us, who shall divide us? Keep us, oh keep us the {{sc|Many in One!}} Up with our banner bright, Sprinkled with starry light, Spread its fair emblems from mountain to shore, While through the sounding sky Loud rings the Nation's cry,— {{sc|Union and Liberty! One evermore!}} </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />SONGS OF WELCOME AND FAREWELL <section end="s3" /> <section begin="s4" />AMERICA TO RUSSIA AUGUST 5, 1866
<poem> Read by Hon. G, V, Vox at a dinner given to ae Mission from the United States, St. Petar- ure.
Tuover watery deserts hold apart ‘The worlds of East and West, Still beats the selisame human heart In each proud Nation’s breust.
Dur floating turret tempts the main And dares the howling blast
To clasp more close fhe golden ehain That Joug has bound them fast.
In vain the gales of ocean sweep, In vain the billows rear
That chafe the wild and stormy steep Of storied Elsinere.
She comes! She comes! her banners dip fo Neva’s flashing tide,
With greetings on her cannon’s lip, The storm-god’s iron bride t
Peace garlands with the olive-bough Her thunder-bearing tower, </poem><section end="s4" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> A Nation gives you smiles unbought At all her opening gates ! : Forgive us when we press your hand, — Your war-worn features scan, — God sent you to a blesding land; Our Nation found its man ! </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />TO H. W, LONGPELLOW
BEFORE HIS DEPARTURE FOR ECROFR, MAY 27, (868
<poem> Our Poet, who has taught the Western breeze To waft his songs before him o'er the seas, Will find them wheresoe'er his wanderings reach Borne on the spreading tide of English speech Twin with the rhythmic waves that kiss the farthest beach.
Where shall the singing bird a stranger be That finds a nest for him in every tree? How shall he travel who can never go Where his own voice the echoes do not know, Where his own garden flowers no longer learn to grow?
Ah! gentlest soul! how gracious, how benign Breathes through our troubled life that voice of thine, Filled with a sweetness born of happier spheres, That wins and warms, that kindles, softens, cheers, That calms the wildest woe and stays the bitterest tears!
Forgive the simple words that sound like praise; The mist before me dims my gilded phrase; Our speech at best is half alive and cold, And save the tenderer moments make us bold Our whitening lips would close, their truest truth untold.
We who behold our autumn sun below The Scorpion's sign, against the Archer's bow, Know well what parting means of friend from friend; After the snows no freshening dews descend, And what the frost has marred, the sunshine will not mend.
So we all count the months, the weeks, the days, That keep thee from us in unwonted ways, Grudging to alien hearths our widowed time; And one has shaped a breath in artless rhyme That sighs, "We track thee still through each remotest clime."
What wishes, longings, blessings, prayers shall be The more than golden freight that floats with thee! And know, whatever welcome thou shalt find,— The proudest, fondest love thou leavest still behind! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s3" />TO CHRISTIAN GOTTFRIED EHRENBERG
FOR HIS “JUBILZUM” AT BERLIN, NO- VEMBER 5, 1868
This poem was written at the suggestion of Mr. George Bancroft, the historian. <poem> Txov who hast taught the teachers of man- kind How from the least of things the might- iest grow, What marvel jealous Nature made thee blind, Lest man should learn what angels long to know ? Thon in the flinty rock, the river’s flow, In the thick-moted sunheam’s sifted light </poem><section end="s3" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><poem> Hast traimed thy downward-pointod tube to shuw Worlds within worlds unveiled to mortal sight, Even as the patient watchers of the night, — The eyclope gleaners of the fruitful skies, — Show the wide misty way where heaven is white ee All paved with sung that daze our won- dering eyes.
Far o'er the stormy decp an empire lics, Beyond the storied islands of the blest, That waits tu see the lingering day-star
rise; The foresi-cinetured Eden of the West; Whose queen, fair Freedom, twines her irou Great With leaves from every wreath that mor- tals wear, Bint loves the sober garland ever heat That science lends the sage’s silvered hair; — Science, who makes life’s heritaga more fair, Forging for every lock its mastering
key, Filling with life and hope the stagnant
air, Ponring the light of Heaven o’er land and sea ! From her unseeptred realm we come te thes Bearing our slender tribute in our hands; Deem it not worthless, humble though it
be, Set by the larger gifts of older lands: The smallest fibres weave the strongest bands, — In usarrowest tubes the sovereign nerves are spui, — A little cord aloug the deep sea-sands Makes the live thought of severed na- tions one: Thy fame has journeyed westering with the sun, Prairics and lone sierras knuw thy name
207
And the long day of service nobly done That erowns thy darkened evening with its flame |
One with the grateful world, we own thy elaim, — Nay, rather claim our right to jomm the throng Who come with varied tongues, but hearts the sanie, Te hail thy festal morn with smiles and song; Ab, happy they to whom the joys belong Of peaceful triumphs that can never die From History’s reeord, —not of gilded wrong, But golden truths that, while the world goes by With all its empty pageant, blazoned high Around the Masler’s name forever shinet So shines thy name illumined ia the sky,— Such joys, such triumphs, such remem-~ brance thine ! </poem> <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />A TOAST TO WILKIE COLLINS
FEBRUARY 16, 1874
<poem> The painter's and the poet's fame Shed their twinned lustre round his name, To gild our story-teller's art, Where each in turn must play his part.
What scenes from Wilkie's pencil sprung, The minstrel saw but left unsung! What shapes the pen of Collins drew, No painter clad in living hue!
But on our artist's shadowy screen A stranger miracle is seen Than priest unveils or pilgrim seeks,— The poem breathes, the picture speaks!
And so his double name comes true, They christened better than they knew, And Art proclaims him twice her son,— Painter and poet, both in one. </poem><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Beleg Âlt" />{{center block/s}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />MEMORIAL VERSES <section end="s1" /> <section begin="s2" />FOR THE SERVICES IN MEMORY OF ABRAHAM LINCOLN
CITY OF BOSTON, JUNE 1, 1865
CHORAL: “LUTHER’S JUDGMENT HYMN
<poem> O thou of soul and sense and breath The ever-present Giver, Unto thy mighty Angel, Death, All flesh thou dost deliver; What most we cherish we resign, For life and death alike are thine, Who reignest Lord forever!
Our hearts lie buried in the dust With him so true and tender, The patriot's stay, the people's trust, The shield of the offender; Yet every murmuring voice is still, As, bowing to thy sovereign will, Our best-loved we surrender.
Dear Lord, with pitying eye behold This martyr generation, Which thou, through trials manifold, Art showing thy salvation! Oh let the blood by murder spilt Wash out thy stricken children's guilt And sanctify our nation!
Be thou thy orphaned Israel's friend, Forsake thy people never, In One our broken Many blend, That none again may sever! Hear us, O Father, while we raise With trembling lips our song of praise, And bless thy name forever! </poem> <section end="s2" /> <section begin="s2" />FOR THE COMMEMORATION SERVICES
CAMBRIDGE, JULY 27, 1865 <poem> Four summers coined their golden ight in leaves, Four wasteful autumna flung them to the gale,
Four winters wore the shroud the tempest 5 Weayes, The fourth wan April weeps o’er hill and vale;
And still the war-clouds scowl on sea and land, With the red gleams of battle staining through, When lo! as parted by an angel's hand, They open, and the heayena again are blue |
Which is the dream, the present or the past ¢
Tho night of anguish or the joyous morn ?
The long, loug years with horrors overcast,
Or the sweet promise of the day new- bern ?
Tell us, O father, as thine arms infeld Thy belted first-born in their fast em- brace, Murmuring the prayer the patriarch breathed of old, — “Now let me die, for I have seen thy
face!”
Tell us, O mother,—nay, thou canst not speak, But thy fond eyes shail answer, brimmed with joy, — Press thy mute lips against the sunbrowned cheek, Is this a phantom, — thy returuing boy ?
Tell us, O maiden, — ah, what canst thon tell That Nature’s record is not first to teach, — The open volume all can read so well, With its twin rose-hued pages full of speech 7?
And ye who mourn your dead,—how aternly trne The crushing hour that wrenched their lives away, Shadowed with sorraw’s midnight yeil fur yon, For them the dawning of immortal day 1 </poem><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}</noinclude>
